title: Developing a Shooters Mentality
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article examines an irrational but persistently effective belief pattern among elite performers: the conviction that misses precede success and successes predict more success, regardless of what statistics actually say about independent events. The author calls this the Shooter's Mentality and argues it functions as a deliberately chosen mindset rather than a factual claim, one that protects fragile confidence from the corrosive effect of self-doubt after failure. The piece is explicit that the science doesn't support the belief, but contends the belief itself measurably improves performance, making its adoption a pragmatic choice rather than a delusion.
points: The Shooter's Mentality is a self-selected belief, not an evidence-based one — performers choose it and hold it despite knowing statistics say otherwise.
Its function is protective: it insulates confidence from the corrosive self-doubt that typically follows a miss or setback.
The mindset applies across domains (sales, negotiation, research, sport), suggesting it's a general performance-psychology tool, not sport-specific superstition.
quotes: Often called a Shooter’s Mentality, the view that good things will follow success and failure is shared among the best performers in every field, even though it isn’t perfectly rational.
They live with two mottos in their heads: “Whenever I miss, it tells me I’m due to make the next shot,” and “Whenever I score, I’m on a streak to score again.
The science may not agree, but it does confirm that the increased confidence produced by a Shooter’s Mentality has a positively profound effect on performance.
Like all beliefs and attitudes, a Shooter’s Mentality is a decision. A performer either insists on holding this belief, regardless of the facts, or they don’t.
Because confidence is both fragile and fickle, they have developed a Shooter’s Mentality to protect themselves against self-doubt.
